title: Constant-pass weighted matching with O(n log n) bits
formal: For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) and fixed integer \(c\geq1\), is there a randomized insertion-only streaming algorithm that, on every \(n\)-vertex simple undirected graph with integer edge weights in \([1,n^c]\), outputs a matching of weight at least \((1-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\) with probability at least \(2/3\), using at most \(p_{\varepsilon,c}\) passes and \(B_{\varepsilon,c}n\log_2(n+2)\) bits of memory, where \(p_{\varepsilon,c},B_{\varepsilon,c}\) do not depend on \(n\)?
why: The question asks whether near-optimal weighted matchings can be found with memory comparable to the explicit output and a fixed number of scans of a dense graph. It isolates the remaining strict memory requirement from the already established existence of constant-pass algorithms with polylogarithmic overhead.
status_note: The broad historical question is substantially resolved: linear-time RAM approximation and constant-pass near-linear-space streaming algorithms exist. This card explicitly retains the stricter O(n log n)-bit streaming variant with polynomially bounded integer weights. The checked general-graph theorems and 2025 overview do not state that precise memory endpoint; no matching resolution was located in the bounded September 2026 check.

progress.text: McGregor poses the streaming approximation and separate RAM-time questions.
Duan and Pettie give a linear-time approximation scheme in the RAM model.
Gamlath and coauthors obtain constant-pass weighted approximation with near-linear memory.
Huang and Su obtain polynomial-in-accuracy pass complexity; Theorem 1.2 records its word-space dependence on the weight ratio.
Assadi’s journal overview compares the available pass-space tradeoffs for weighted and unweighted matching.

importance.reason: A precise resource question for a fundamental graph optimization task; its historical RAM and broad semi-streaming components are separated from the stricter bit-space endpoint.

sentences: The input is an arbitrary-order insertion stream of a positively weighted general graph.
The algorithm must output a nearly maximum-weight matching after a number of passes independent of graph size.
The retained space target is O(n log n) bits with polynomially bounded integer weights.
Linear-time RAM approximation and broader constant-pass semi-streaming results are already known.
The card distinguishes those achievements from the exact bit-space endpoint it asks to settle.

definitions: The vertex set is \([n]\). A matching is a subset of edges with no shared endpoint, its weight is the sum of its edge weights, and \(\operatorname{OPT}\) is the largest such sum over all matchings of the graph. The input is a list of distinct edges, each represented by two binary vertex identifiers and its positive binary integer weight. The algorithm knows \(n,\varepsilon,c\). It reads the list sequentially in an arbitrary order selected independently of its random choices. A pass reads the same complete list in that same order; no deletions, changes of order, random access to earlier items, or requests for selected edges are allowed. The algorithm may stop after any number of passes up to the stated bound. At the end it must output the actual edges of a matching, not merely an estimate of its value. The empty graph has optimum zero and admits the empty output. All stored bits, including edge identifiers, weights, random seeds retained for reuse, counters and temporary working memory, count toward space. A final write-only output tape is permitted, but cannot be used as storage during the passes. The bound is worst case over inputs and random choices; success is required for each input and order. Local computation time is unrestricted, and the finite algorithm may depend on the fixed accuracy and weight exponent. Equivalently the space target is O(n) words of O(log n) bits for each fixed pair of parameters. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) is required for the pass count or space constant.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm and proof of the approximation, actual matching output, pass and bit-space guarantees for every fixed accuracy and weight exponent. Alternatively prove that this family of guarantees is impossible, for some fixed parameters. A constant-pass algorithm with extra logarithmic factors in bits, an algorithm for bipartite graphs only, or a RAM approximation algorithm does not establish the displayed statement.

context_blocks.text: The 2006 page contains two questions: a constant-pass streaming approximation with O(n log n) space, and a linear-time RAM approximation scheme. This card keeps the streaming question as its single target. Editorial convention: space is measured explicitly in bits and weights have polynomially bounded integer encodings, removing an ambiguity in the historical page.

Duan and Pettie resolved the RAM direction with running time \(O(m\varepsilon^{-1}\log\varepsilon^{-1})\) for maximum-weight matching. That algorithm can access and store the graph in ways unavailable to the streaming model. The old RAM question is therefore recorded as solved context rather than repeated as an open demand.

Gamlath, Kale, Mitrović and Svensson obtained arbitrarily accurate weighted matching in a number of passes depending only on accuracy, using memory linear in n up to polylogarithmic factors. This settles the broader constant-pass semi-streaming objective, but the stated space guarantee alone does not supply the exact bit bound retained here.

Huang and Su improve the number of passes to a polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\). Their Theorem 1.2 states \(O(n\log W\,\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon))\) words, where \(W\) is the weight ratio. Under the present weight encoding this can be \(O_{\varepsilon,c}(n\log^2 n)\) bits. One must account for word size before comparing it with the target.

The 2025 overview distinguishes general weighted graphs from bipartite and unweighted cases and tabulates their different pass-space guarantees. Strong bounds for one of those restrictions cannot be silently substituted for the graph class here.

For weighted matchings, improving the objective can involve both alternating paths and alternating cycles. Retaining enough information to coordinate such improvements while storing only a linear number of words is the specific resource issue in this formulation.
